analysis.one_liner: Expands housing, insurance, job, and legal protections for victims of domestic violence.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 105th Congress, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given federal housing vouchers to families forced from their homes by domestic violence, barred insurers from denying or canceling coverage because someone is a victim of abuse, and made it illegal to fire or penalize workers because they are victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. It also would have funded free legal help and shelters for victims, protected abused immigrant women from losing food stamps and housing aid, and let victims change their Social Security numbers and get unemployment benefits or leave from work to deal with the abuse. The bill was introduced near the end of the 105th Congress and never received any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, and stalking — mostly women and their children. The bill would have created $50 million in new Section 8 housing vouchers for families fleeing abuse, provided grants of $23 million in fiscal 1999 rising to $57 million in fiscal 2001 for free legal representation, increased shelter funding through fiscal 2003, and created a national clearinghouse to help employers assist victimized workers. Victims would have gained the right to sue insurers who deny them coverage or charge them more because of abuse, the right to sue employers who fire or discriminate against them, guaranteed unemployment benefits if abuse forced them from a job, protected leave to deal with the abuse, new Social Security numbers, and waivers from rigid welfare and immigration rules for battered immigrant women and their children. Employers would also have gained a 40% tax credit for the cost of workplace safety programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of domestic violence and their children

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $50 million in new Section 8 housing assistance, provided only to public housing agencies and nonprofits, for families who must leave their homes because of domestic violence, with open-ended funding authorized after fiscal 1999.

Prohibits insurers from denying, canceling, or limiting coverage, or adding premium surcharges, because a person is or may be a victim of abuse; blocks coverage termination when a victim loses the abuser's plan; and gives victims a private right to sue in state or federal court, with $5,000 statutory damages per violation and FTC enforcement.

Authorizes grants — $23 million in fiscal 1999, $44 million in 2000, and $57 million in 2001 — for free and low-cost legal representation for victims of domestic violence regardless of sexual orientation or immigration status, with at least 5% reserved for tribal organizations.

Makes it unlawful for employers to refuse to hire, fire, or discriminate against workers because they are victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, or because they seek a safety accommodation like a schedule change, transfer, or new lock; victims can recover lost wages, compensatory damages, and up to triple actual damages in punitive damages, plus reinstatement.

Requires unemployment compensation for workers who lose jobs as a direct result of domestic violence, entitles employees to leave to address the abuse, requires claims reviewers trained in domestic violence dynamics, and gives employers a 40% tax credit for workplace safety programs such as escorts, security equipment, counseling, and legal help for victims.
Increases and extends appropriations for battered women's shelters and state domestic violence coalitions through fiscal 2003, and funds emergency assistance funds administered by state coalitions.

Restores eligibility for food stamps, housing assistance, welfare, and work authorization to battered immigrant women, lets them count an abusive spouse's work quarters after divorce, waives deportation in narrow circumstances, and removes fees for their immigration petitions.

Lets verified victims of domestic violence change their Social Security numbers, lets states grant TANF compliance waivers to victims without penalty, and extends child-support disclosure protections to situations of unreasonable risk to a parent or child.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the housing vouchers, legal-aid grants, shelter funding, and clearinghouse. Insurers would bear new anti-discrimination obligations across health, life, disability, and property coverage, written privacy protocols, and lawsuits carrying $5,000 statutory damages per violation. Employers would face a new employment-discrimination ban with damages up to triple actual losses, mandatory unemployment compensation paid through state systems, and new leave obligations — partially offset by a 40% tax credit for qualifying safety programs, which itself reduces federal revenue.

drawbacks.text: The spending is partly open-ended: the $50 million housing authorization grows to 'such sums as may be necessary' after fiscal 1999, legal-aid grants rise to $57 million a year, and shelter funding is extended through fiscal 2003.

The private right of action against insurers — with $5,000 statutory damages for each violation and attorney's fees — plus employment suits allowing up to triple punitive damages would expose insurers and employers to substantial new litigation.

One provision lets the Attorney General waive deportation for a first-time domestic violence offender who is separated from the victim and current on court-ordered child support, which critics could reasonably argue softens consequences for abusers.
Mandating unemployment compensation for separations caused by domestic violence shifts costs onto state unemployment systems and the employers who finance them.

The 40% employer tax credit for workplace safety programs adds another revenue cost to the Treasury, and because only two senators backed the bill, it never received any hearing or analysis of how the provisions would work in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's premise is well supported: economic dependence is a major reason victims stay with abusers, and the bill's own findings cite surveys that over half of battered women stayed because they lacked resources to leave. Its tools — housing vouchers, legal representation, insurance and job protections, and safe access to benefits — aim directly at that dependence. The costs are real but targeted: new spending of roughly $75-125 million a year across programs, plus compliance and litigation exposure for insurers and employers, partially offset by an employer tax credit. The bill was never debated or amended, so design questions — the open-ended housing authorization, the abuser deportation waiver, and the breadth of the statutory damages — were never tested. As written, the help it would deliver to a vulnerable population outweighs its costs, but it was never vetted enough to know for certain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999, so it died quietly.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the Battered Women's Economic Security Act on October 6, 1998, joined by Senator Paul Wellstone as its only cosponsor; the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The referral came in the closing weeks of the second session of the 105th Congress, and the Judiciary Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired with it, never reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and employers were spared the new anti-discrimination duties, damages exposure, and leave mandates the bill would have imposed, and the federal government avoided the new spending. Domestic violence victims, who would have gained housing, legal, insurance, and job protections, received nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers avoided new mandates

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on October 6, 1998.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on October 6, 1998 — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup before the session adjourned.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and only the two Democratic sponsors are on record, so no partisan split on the bill itself can be measured; it died in a Republican-run committee without any recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Health, life, disability, and property insurers
industries.note: The bill would bar insurers from denying, canceling, or limiting coverage, or charging higher premiums, because an applicant is a victim of abuse, and would require strict confidentiality around abuse records. Victims could sue for $5,000 per violation, so the industry's ability to screen out abuse-related risk — which keeps those victims uninsured — would end.

Employers would face a ban on firing or penalizing victims, mandatory unemployment compensation and leave for abuse-related separations, and lawsuits with up to triple punitive damages. The same bill hands them a 40% tax credit for workplace safety and victim-assistance programs.

industries.industry: Domestic violence shelters, legal services, and advocacy nonprofits
industries.note: The bill steers new federal money to these organizations — legal-aid grants up to $57 million a year, increased shelter funding through fiscal 2003, and a $500,000-a-year national clearinghouse grant — making them the delivery channel for most of the bill's services.
Public housing agencies (alongside qualified nonprofits) would exclusively administer the new $50 million in tenant-based housing vouchers for families fleeing abuse.
